#9823. ToyBlocks: A controlled world for robot learning and evaluation

💻 Code | 📊 Data | 🤖 Models | 📖 Documentation

Robots are learning to fold laundry, sort parts, and handle unfamiliar objects. But those demonstrations are often rather narrow and don't explain what a robot has learned or why it fails.

To study a complex system, scientists often begin with a small, controlled environment, such as a petri dish or terrarium, where they can vary conditions and observe the effects. Robotics needs environments that make this kind of investigation possible—researchers should be able to change the training data or model design, repeat a test, and trace the cause of a failure.

Today we're introducing a framework for creating these environments; we call them FoundationWorlds. Each pairs a controlled, simulated world targeted at studying robotics in a specific environment with tools for automatically generating tasks and training demonstrations, as well as metrics for measuring a robot's behavior over time. Together, they provide a setting for studying questions such as how models improve as more training data becomes available, and how to best combine high-level reasoning with precise physical control.

Our first foundation world is ToyBlocks: an open simulation framework built around a robot arm and blocks on a tabletop. The setting is deliberately simple, but the robot must still reason about how the blocks interact and how to arrange them while pushing, flipping, and stacking.

ToyBlocks automatically generates demonstrations, which are recordings of a robot completing tasks in simulation, without requiring time-consuming teleoperation, in which a person remotely controls the robot. Researchers can easily vary these training experiences. For example, a team could generate more pushing or flipping demonstrations, then evaluate performance on tasks kept out of training.

Starting with ToyBlocks as our first FoundationWorld, we aim to extend the approach to increasingly complex environments.

Building on our earlier work in open robot learning, including MolmoAct 2, MolmoBot, and MolmoSpaces, ToyBlocks gives researchers a way to study robotics questions in a deliberately constrained domain.

As a FoundationWorld, ToyBlocks is designed around four requirements: (1) realistic physics and appearance, (2) automatic generation of tasks and demonstrations at scale, (3) challenges that combine reasoning with dexterity, and (4) broad coverage of the tasks possible within a domain.

Open-ended domains require modeling a wide range of objects and interactions, making it infeasible to fulfill all these requirements. ToyBlocks’ narrow scope, on the other hand, makes it possible to fulfill them all.

Within ToyBlocks' smaller setting, researchers can work toward investigating how a robot can learn to perform any reasonable task while being confident that the simulated arm and blocks behave very similarly to their physical counterparts.

A physical robot gripper above wooden blocks in the ToyBlocks setup.

ToyBlocks is not just about picking and stacking blocks: pictures and letters on the blocks' faces allow for searching, sorting, and arranging tasks. A robot may need to turn a block to see a hidden face before deciding where it belongs. Domain randomization – varying block size, table height, and other physical properties from scene to scene – tests how well models generalize as the geometry changes.

ToyBlocks automatically generates skills (behaviors for short tasks) and task demonstrations that can be used to train models or adapt previously trained models through additional training (fine-tuning). High-level reasoning models decide what to do; low-level action models control the robot’s movements. The framework can also be used to easily design experiments and validate hypotheses.

ToyBlocks uses reinforcement learning (RL) and motion planning, which computes how the robot should move, to generate skills for short-horizon tasks, which involve brief sequences of actions. Skill training takes place in Isaac Lab, Nvidia's open-source framework for robot learning in simulation. Through trial and error, these policies – models that choose the robot’s actions – learn non-prehensile skills such as pushing a block across the table or flipping it onto another face without picking it up. Skill generation can draw on privileged information – values the simulator can supply directly but a real robot cannot, such as a block's exact position and orientation – instead of estimating it from camera images. This enables the automatic generation of skills that would require teleoperation in the real world.

To generate demonstration data, a task-and-motion planner (TAMP) automatically selects and sequences the skills needed to solve a task and plans the robot’s movements between them. Running each plan in simulation produces a dataset of recorded demonstrations along with labels describing which task or skill the robot performs. ToyBlocks scales data generation through generating and executing hundreds of such plans in parallel on a single graphics processing unit (GPU), reaching up to 24 times real-time performance.

Acting from sensor observations adds a perception problem: a model has to estimate a block’s pose – its position and orientation – which the simulator could supply directly. To reflect real-world conditions, ToyBlocks trains models that map raw sensor observations to actions.

Execution of Molmo 2 (a high-level model) and ManiFlow (a low-level model) trained in ToyBlocks. Molmo 2 selects skills such as rotation and flipping, indicating the relevant block via a pointing interface, while ManiFlow controls the simulated arm to execute the commanded skills.

ToyBlocks' controllable data generator lets users create training mixtures that emphasize particular skills or fill gaps in existing datasets. Researchers can study how much data a model needs and which experiences help it generalize to unseen tasks. For example, they could test whether adding rotation and pick-and-place demonstrations improves flipping, or vary the balance of examples inside and outside a defined workspace region—evaluating their choices on tasks kept out of training. Importantly, evaluation of trained models generates metrics beyond success rates; it provides information such as execution speeds, forces exerted on objects, and task progress measured via the same specifications used by the planning module.

A webpage interface lets users connect Claude – or another frontier model – and use natural language to instruct the robot or try tasks, offering a way to explore how a model plans and acts without needing robotics expertise.

The evaluations below use ToyBlocks to study how training data and methods affect performance, spatial reasoning, generalization to new letters and block appearances, multi-step planning, transfer to physical robots, and frontier models that act through tools. Users can easily design their own tasks and measures to investigate other questions—for example, whether a model performs better when it selects objects by pointing or by issuing text commands such as "pick the yellow block."

Low-level action models, such as vision-language-action models (VLAs), map language instructions and visual observations to robot actions.

The premise of VLAs is that, by pretraining on large-scale datasets, they can rapidly generalize to different scenarios or a specific workspace. However, evidence on how well these action models generalize remains conflicting. Some studies report that these action models are brittle to changes in inputs, such as different object layouts and lighting, whereas others show that VLAs generalize well. We argue that these studies often rely on real-world datasets with limited flexibility in spatial variations. ToyBlocks enables us to test how well action models generalize in a simple, easily reproducible setting with meaningful task-space diversity.

We design generalization tests that vary the skill sequences needed to complete an instruction, the letters or colors on the blocks, and the number of blocks in a scene. A stacking study can withhold four-block stacks from training, then test whether a model can combine familiar movements to build them. Workspace studies distinguish performance at new positions within a training region from performance beyond its boundaries, where the model has to extrapolate. We illustrate the study setup and findings below.

We consider four tasks: Stack, Unstack, Flip, and Rotate. For these tasks, we study interpolation (new configurations within the training range) and extrapolation (configurations beyond that range). For example, we evaluate generalization by training on scenarios where objects spawn only in the left region (green) and testing on the right region (orange), or by training on stack heights of 2 and 5 blocks and testing on heights 3 and 4.

Spatial generalization studies for VLA models (results based on ManiFlow, π0.5, and MolmoAct 2). Despite large-scale pretraining, these popular action models generalize poorly in the initial results. We improve generalization and analyze the contribution of each technique. The chart’s LoRA label stands for low-rank adaptation, a method for fine-tuning a model with a small set of trainable weight updates. We believe action model generalization remains far from solved; ToyBlocks provides a valuable testbed for systematically exploring generalization techniques.

Long-horizon tasks, which require many steps, allow us to measure how well models can plan a sequence of actions to solve them. Our framework enables us to create such long-horizon tasks, and create oracles – reference components that provide correct plans or actions – at both the high and low levels. This allows us to isolate whether the high-level planning or low-level execution failed when a model fails at a task. An example long-horizon task might be to spell “Ai2” with a block stack; because the letters may not be immediately visible, the agent must first choose actions that reveal information, and then plan and execute a sequence of actions to build the stack.

We evaluate hierarchical models with explicit high-level planning and low-level execution models. In this instance, we choose Molmo 2, a vision-language model (VLM), as the high-level planner, and ManiFlow as the low-level policy. Molmo 2 chooses the skill to execute and the block to execute it on, while the low-level model executes the instruction. We train low-level models such as ManiFlow to pause after completing the execution and query the high-level model for the next instruction. We evaluate the model’s planning abilities on three scenarios of increasing difficulty. The easiest scenario initializes with each character upright and facing the camera. The medium scenario has characters that may not be upright, and the hardest scenario contains characters that are not visible at the start of the episode.

Success rates on three-letter block-spelling tasks using Molmo 2 as the high-level reasoning model and either ManiFlow or a motion planner for low-level manipulation. An example task is “Stack Ai2”. Molmo 2 and ManiFlow are trained on ToyBlocks and evaluated across three difficulty settings and two generalization conditions.

Our experiments with agentic systems test how frontier models plan and act through tool calls. We study three settings using Claude Opus 5.5. In the search-and-spell setting, we expose ToyBlocks skills through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), a standard for connecting AI applications to tools. The agent sees the scene through camera images, calls skills such as pick, flip, or rotate by pointing at a pixel, and decides when to search, build, or declare the task complete or impossible. The same MCP tools can execute either the scripted skills that generate ToyBlocks demonstrations (motion-planned pick and place, plus RL-based rotate and flip) or learned ManiFlow skills. ToyBlocks includes the framework behind these experiments, which also powers the natural-language web interface described earlier.

A frontier model (Claude Fable 5.1) controls a robot in a ToyBlocks world to search for and stack blocks into a tower spelling “Ai2.” During the episode, the agent muses, “I need to figure out whether pick-and-place naturally straightens orientation or if I need to correct it manually… I have 63 calls left, plenty to run a controlled test” (0:06). The agent later hypothesizes: “…maybe the gripper’s yaw is radial—pointing from the robot base toward the block” (0:15) and eventually confirms this hypothesis (0:26) before constructing the three-block tower, but the ‘A’ is sideways (1:11). Surprisingly, current frontier models often make similar perceptual errors (see the next figure), despite their impressive planning, spatial reasoning, and search capabilities.

For classical planning, the agent (our system using Claude Opus 5.5 to plan and choose actions) solves all 30 of a group of block-stacking tasks similar to ones that frontier models struggled with a few years ago, using text descriptions. It also solves 30 out of 30 while repeatedly observing camera images and choosing its next action in a closed loop.

In the search-and-spell setting, the agent had to generate stacks spelling out three-letter words. It had to find the blocks with the corresponding letters among up to eight blocks in the scene. Importantly, 50% of the scenes did not have blocks with all the required letters, rendering the task infeasible. In this case, we required the agent to state that the task is infeasible. We found that in this experiment, the agent was able to successfully solve or correctly declare infeasible 63% of the tasks. Errors were mostly caused by the agent confusing letters with look-alike letters (13%) or choosing an incorrect orientation for a letter in a stack (15%).

Our results also show that the agent was able to solve the task more efficiently when the blocks had semantic regularities, or patterns, taking advantage of such patterns to reason about occluded faces. For instance, in most of the infeasible scenes, when the blocks had no patterns, the agent correctly looked at all the blocks’ faces before declaring infeasibility, whereas it was able to declare infeasibility significantly faster when the blocks had semantic patterns.

Our third experimental setting asks whether an agent can learn how its skills behave, using experiments as a scientist would. When a skill behaves unexpectedly, the agent forms a hypothesis, designs a small test, and revises its understanding from the result. We expand on this idea by having an agent run its own experiments and write its own skill descriptions based on what it finds. These learned descriptions raise success rates from 24% with the default descriptions to 63%, outperforming the 36% achieved with descriptions written by a human expert.

Share of letter-block faces the agent had exposed by the end of each “search and spell” episode (bars averaged over 20 episodes; one marker per episode, styled by outcome). In a feasible task every letter of the three-letter target word is present; in an infeasible task, one letter is missing and the agent should say so. Each patterned block carries uppercase and lowercase instances of a letter, plus images that begin with the letter (e.g., A-block: apple, ant, A, 1, airplane, a); an unpatterned block’s six faces are randomized and unrelated. Correct: the tower spelled the word, or for infeasible tasks, the agent correctly declared the task impossible. Letter rotated or look-alike: the agent built the tower, but a letter was turned or a look-alike substituted, including five infeasible tasks declared solved with a look-alike in the missing letter’s place. Block fell out of reach; reported: a needed block was pushed out of the arm’s reach, so the agent reported that its task had become impossible. No report: the agent used up its motor-skill budget and stopped without claiming either outcome. With patterned blocks, the agent finishes having seen fewer faces, because it can infer what hidden faces must depict rather than checking every one.

Action-conditioned world models are trained to predict how a scene changes in response to a robot’s actions. Using them as an alternative to model-based simulators for training and evaluating robot policies is an active area of research. How well they serve this purpose depends on how accurately they predict physical interactions, which is hard to measure without knowing the true state of the scene. ToyBlocks provides this ground truth – the actual simulated scene state – enabling highly controlled tests of how recently developed world models perform in low-level object manipulation. Here, the arm’s end effector is its gripper.

Specifically, we tested whether action-conditioned world models are capable of predicting the motions of blocks or the outcomes of skill executions after being trained on example executions. To do so, we chose four different skills (pick-and-place, flip, rotate, and a mixed task) and generated 900 trajectories – sequences of robot states and actions over time – for each skill. 50% of these trajectories were successful demonstrations of the skill, and 50% were unsuccessful because of small changes to spatial configurations. With equal numbers of successful and unsuccessful executions, a model that always predicts success would be correct only half the time. The models were fine-tuned on these demonstrations and then tested on their ability to predict the outcome of action sequences of the same skills.

We find that Wan 2.2 predicts block motion and task outcomes most accurately. Astra tracks the gripper well but struggles to simulate contact. LeWM is fast and more accurate over short interaction segments, though it drifts over full trajectories. In additional experiments, we also showed that models that score higher on pose and success prediction also produce better training data: adding 100 model-generated trajectories (rollouts) from the best video-generation model raises a policy’s success in an unseen region from 19% to 78%.

We tested three types of models: a video prediction model with 5 billion parameters (Wan 2.2), an agentic model that created its own physics simulator tuned to match the demonstration data (Astra), and a latent world model (LeWM). During testing, each trained model has to predict future images, simulator states, or latent states (learned internal representations), respectively, based on an initial image and a sequence of actions. For full trajectories, models use the initial image as the only observed image, along with the action sequence. For short interaction segments – a single pick, place, flip, or rotate – models start from the real image immediately before that interaction. Full trajectories show how errors accumulate over long horizons, while interaction segments isolate a single interaction, such as the gripper making contact with a block, and show how well the model predicts it. To compare models fairly, we probe each model’s predictions, reading out where it expects the blocks and gripper to be at different points in the trajectory and whether it expects the task to succeed at the end.

Sim-to-real evaluations test policies trained in simulation on physical robots performing block manipulation tasks. By comparing simulation and real-world execution, we assess whether behaviors and failure patterns observed in simulation provide meaningful indications of real-world performance. For example, researchers can evaluate individual skills and their composition in longer-horizon tasks to identify where failures arise and whether these patterns carry over to physical deployments.

We test whether the models trained entirely on ToyBlocks simulation datasets can be deployed in the real world zero-shot, without training on real-world examples. We evaluate ManiFlow and each low-level skill (pick, place, flip, and rotate) individually. We test whether the hierarchical system (Molmo 2 + ManiFlow) can complete long-horizon three-block spelling tasks requiring sequences of these actions. Real-world experiments use a Franka FR3 arm with a Robotiq gripper across thirty scene configurations. Each scene contains 4–10 blocks seen during training. An episode is successful only if the relevant blocks are moved to target poses without collisions. If the operator intervenes to stop the robot due to an unsafe motion during an episode, it is marked as a failure.

ManiFlow’s atomic-skill success rates were similar in simulation and the real world (80.0% and 81.1%). The hierarchical Molmo 2 + ManiFlow system succeeded in 55.5% of simulated episodes (111/200) and 50.0% of real-world episodes (15/30); further trials are needed to establish statistical confidence across tasks.

Success rates of the ManiFlow low-level model and the hierarchical Molmo 2–ManiFlow system in simulation and the real world. For ManiFlow, the total count represents individual skill executions (pick, place, flip, and rotate), whereas for Molmo 2–ManiFlow, it represents block-spelling task episodes. The Molmo 2–ManiFlow evaluations use the easiest scene configuration defined in the simulation evaluation, with block characters visible and upright.

Side-by-side real-world and simulated block-stacking executions using the same high-level planner. Pink rings mark the planner’s target point for each skill. The scenes use different block labels, and simulation playback is retimed to align grasps and releases with the real robot.

To transfer Molmo 2 and ManiFlow – both trained exclusively on ToyBlocks data – to a physical robot, we address the differences between simulation and reality in three stages.

Before data generation, we perform system identification by tuning simulated robot parameters, including joint friction and armature (the motor and gearbox inertia reflected at the joint), to match real-robot trajectories. During data generation, we randomize physical properties (object size, friction, and table height) and visual properties (lighting, backgrounds, materials, and camera parameters). At inference time, observations are captured using a front-facing ZED camera and a wrist-mounted ZED Mini. For policies that use depth images, we generate clean depth maps, which estimate distance at each pixel, from paired red-green-blue (RGB) camera images using FastFoundationStereo, rather than relying on noisy depth sensor measurements.

The physical ToyBlocks setup: a robot arm, wooden blocks, and a camera.

ToyBlocks connects data generation, training, and evaluation in one controlled setting, so researchers can investigate how robots learn over time and test how changes to a model or its training data affect robot behavior. We’re releasing simulation assets, procedural task and demonstration generators, automatically generated demonstrations, two trained models showcasing what the framework can do (one based on Molmo 2 and one based on ManiFlow), training code, and evaluation code and validation sets. This allows other teams to build their own training mixtures and investigate failure modes beyond those covered in our initial experiments.

Our initial data release is a proof point with 85,336 long-horizon demonstrations, each comprising about 6–12 skill demonstrations, depending on the set. The initial datasets cover nearly 1,600 hours of robot execution data and 144 million frames. In a few weeks, we're targeting a second release with a larger-scale dataset, more skills, and more comprehensive benchmarking. We’ll also add fully integrated RL training capability that is not contained in the current package.

Other directions for ToyBlocks include bimanual (two-arm) manipulation and dexterous robot hands, equipped with force and touch sensors for studying motion and tasks that involve frequent physical contact. We're also exploring play with unstructured piles of blocks as a way to collect data and study how new behaviors and tasks might emerge through interaction.

Future direction: RL-based pile manipulation.

Future direction: bimanual block manipulation.

With ToyBlocks, we want to advance the science of robot learning toward a future where robots can reliably apply what they've learned to unfamiliar tasks and environments. We encourage the research community to explore ToyBlocks for their own investigations and even as a basis to build their own FoundationWorlds.

#9822. osFoundry कैसे पहचानता है कि Claude Code किसी permission prompt पर रुका है?

जब Claude Code 2.1.303 कोई command चलाने की अनुमति माँगता है, तो वह अपने terminal में यह लिखता है। ये bytes एक असली capture से हैं, जिसे osFoundry test fixture के रूप में रखता है (resources/agent-detection/fixtures/claude.blocked.raw):

(पढ़ने में आसानी के लिए line breaks जोड़े गए हैं। असली capture में कोई line break नहीं है।)

इसमें दो चीज़ें ऐसी हैं जो सबसे सीधा detector तोड़ देती हैं। "Do" और "you" के बीच कोई space नहीं है। \x1b[5G cursor को column 5 पर ले जाता है, और "space" बस एक ऐसा cell है जिसे छुआ ही नहीं गया। और कहीं भी \n नहीं है: हर row \r और cursor-down \x1b[1B से शुरू होती है। fixture फ़ोल्डर के सभी 11 Claude Code captures (हर एक 2,099 से 7,672 bytes) में एक भी newline byte नहीं है।

osFoundry का डेस्कटॉप ऐप अपने Sessions board के हर terminal pane के लिए यह सवाल हल करता है: "क्या यह agent मेरा इंतज़ार कर रहा है?" नीचे बताया गया है कि वह क्या करता है, क्यों करता है, और एक छोटा Python supervisor है जो एक live PTY पर तीन आम तरीकों (prompt patterns, output-idle timers, process state) की तुलना करता है। इस Mac पर claude binary नहीं है, इसलिए live हिस्सा एक fake agent चलाता है जो Claude Code के prompt के शब्द और redraw करने का तरीका कॉपी करता है। fixture वाला हिस्सा असली captured bytes इस्तेमाल करता है।

हर agent के लिए एक TOML फ़ाइल। Claude Code की फ़ाइल apps/web/src-tauri/resources/agent-detection/claude.toml है, और यही फ़ाइल https://osfoundry.io/agent-detection/claude.toml पर भी मिलती है। इसके rules, क्रम से:

जो rule सबसे पहले match होता है वही जीतता है (runtime/detect.rs में CompiledManifest::evaluate)। blocked सबसे ऊपर है, क्योंकि prompt खुला होने पर भी Claude Code के footer में "esc to interrupt" लिखा रहता है। अगर working पहले test होता, तो prompt कभी दिखता ही नहीं। जिस screen पर कोई rule match नहीं होता, उसे idle बताया जाता है, कभी blocked नहीं।

फ़ाइल के comments बताते हैं कि क्या हटाया गया और क्यों। Would you like to हटा दिया गया, क्योंकि यह Codex के prompt के शब्द हैं, और Claude के आम जवाबों में "Would you like me to…" बार-बार आता है।

runtime/mod.rs हर write पर classify करने के बजाय हर 700 ms (SWEEP_INTERVAL) पर सभी panes का एक sweep चलाता है। spinner एक सेकंड में कई बार redraw होता है, तो हर write पर classify करने का मतलब होता एक ही जवाब पाने के लिए सेकंड में सैकड़ों बार regex चलाना।

ऊपर वाले bytes की वजह से। यहाँ rules को Python में port करके हर Claude Code fixture पर दो तरीकों से चलाया गया है। पहला तरीका आख़िरी 8 KB लेता है, escape sequences हटाता है, और हर line में आख़िरी \r के बाद का text रखता है। दूसरा तरीका bytes को 32×120 के screen emulator (लगभग 100 lines, नीचे vt.py) में डालता है और rows वापस पढ़ता है।

stripped tail सारे idle सही सिर्फ़ इसलिए बताता है क्योंकि idle fallback है। उसे prompt कभी दिखता ही नहीं। \n न होने से पूरा capture एक ही "line" बन जाता है, और आख़िरी \r के बाद का text रखने से आख़िरी टुकड़े के अलावा सब फेंक दिया जाता है। उस step के बिना भी शब्द आपस में चिपके हुए निकलते हैं: Doyouwanttoproceed?।

osFoundry का code भी यही कहता है। terminal_pty.rs हर session के लिए एक vt100::Parser रखता है, और sweep सिर्फ़ screen_text() को, यानी emulated screen को, classify करता है। उसके ऊपर रखी 200 rows की history जानबूझकर बाहर रखी गई है। वहाँ का comment कहता है कि जिस prompt का user जवाब दे चुका है और जो ऊपर scroll हो चुका है, वह "would report the agent as blocked forever"।

emulator का बहुत अच्छा होना ज़रूरी नहीं। यह वाला text, \r \n \b, cursor moves (A B C D E F G H f d) और erase (J K) संभालता है, और colours, modes और OSC titles को छोड़ देता है। यह हर cell में एक character रखता है, तो कोई wide glyph एक column खिसका सकता है। पूरी rows पर चलने वाले regex को इससे फ़र्क नहीं पड़ता। यह सभी 11 captures को rules के लिए काफ़ी ठीक render करता है:

ज़्यादातर लोग सबसे पहले यही detector लिखते हैं: अगर agent ने N सेकंड तक कुछ print नहीं किया, तो शायद उसे आपकी ज़रूरत है। इसे screen rules के सामने परखने के लिए एक supervisor agent को PTY में चलाता है और हर 50 ms पर log करता है कि हर detector क्या सोचता है।

agent है fake_agent.py, एक stand-in, क्योंकि इस Mac पर कोई claude binary installed नहीं है। यह वे आदतें कॉपी करता है जो मायने रखती हैं:

यह अपनी असली state एक side file में लिखता है जिसे सिर्फ़ scorer पढ़ता है। एक bot user बनकर हर prompt का जवाब उसके आने के 3 से 8 s बाद देता है, और turn ख़त्म होने के 3 से 10 s बाद अगला task type करता है। supervisor का मुख्य हिस्सा, छोटा करके:

seed 7 के साथ एक run: 30 tasks, 10.6 मिनट, 25 permission prompts, और उन पर इंतज़ार में 144 s। Latency वह समय है जो prompt draw होने से लेकर detector के "needs you" कहने तक लगता है। Linger यह है कि जवाब देने के बाद भी detector कितनी देर तक यही कहता रहा। false alarms को episodes / कुल सेकंड के रूप में गिना गया है, और इस हिसाब से बाँटा गया है कि agent असल में क्या कर रहा था।

idle timer के लिए कोई भी threshold काम नहीं करता। परिभाषा से ही उसकी latency उसका threshold है। 5 s से कम पर यह हर silent tool call पर fire होता है। 3 s तक के हर threshold पर यह सभी 30 turn ends पर fire होता है, क्योंकि "काम ख़त्म, अगले task का इंतज़ार" उतना ही शांत है जितना "permission का इंतज़ार"। 5 s और उससे ऊपर यह ऐसे prompts चूकने लगता है जिनका जवाब किसी ने समय पर दे दिया। 8 s वाली row सभी 25 सिर्फ़ इसलिए चूकती है क्योंकि bot कभी 8 s से ज़्यादा इंतज़ार नहीं करता, लेकिन जवाब देने का समय कुछ भी हो, pattern वही रहता है: detector या तो शोर करता है या देर से आता है।

"?" पर ख़त्म होने वाली screen line हर prompt पकड़ लेती है, और असली captures पर यह perfect दिखती: सिर्फ़ चार blocked fixtures में ऐसी line है। live run में यह agent के अपने सवाल, "Would you like me to add a regression test?", पर fire होती है, और वह line अगले task तक screen पर बनी रहती है। claude.toml ने Would you like to इसी वजह से हटाया था।

stripped tail इस run में prompts इसलिए पकड़ पाता है क्योंकि fake agent ❯ 1. Yes असली spaces के साथ लिखता है। फिर जवाब के बाद भी यह औसतन 77 s तक prompt report करता रहता है, क्योंकि मिटाए गए prompt के bytes आख़िरी 8 KB में तब तक रहते हैं जब तक लगभग 8 KB नया output उन्हें बाहर न धकेल दे। spinner के 600 bytes प्रति सेकंड और बीच के silent हिस्सों के साथ इसमें काफ़ी समय लगता है। emulated screen cursor-up और erase आते ही prompt भूल जाती है।

700 ms sweep की कीमत वही है जिसकी उम्मीद होगी: एक interval तक की latency (median 0.26 s, max 0.70 s) और एक interval तक का linger। जिस badge को कोई इंसान देखता है, उसके लिए यह ठीक है।

macOS पर नहीं। supervisor ने agent के लिए सेकंड में दो बार ps -o stat=,time= sample किया:

अपने terminal पर read() में blocked process और spinner frames के बीच सो रहा process, दोनों S हैं। wchan column, जो कुछ systems पर kernel wait channel का नाम बताता है, दोनों के लिए - print करता है। CPU time से भी फ़र्क नहीं पता चलता, क्योंकि spinner का ख़र्च लगभग शून्य है। Claude Code जैसा Node-based CLI काम करते हुए भी और न करते हुए भी अपने event loop में इंतज़ार करता है, तो उसका state letter और भी कम बताएगा।

process table जिस सवाल का जवाब देती है, वह यह है कि terminal किस program के पास है। osFoundry runtime/signals.rs में tty का foreground process group (MasterPty::process_group_leader, यानी tcgetpgrp) पढ़ता है। इससे उसे पता चलता है कि pane में claude चल रहा है, भले ही उसे किसी सामान्य shell में type किया गया हो। इससे यह भी पता चलता है कि agent कब exit हो गया और shell वापस सामने आ गया, जबकि agent का आख़िरी prompt अभी भी screen पर है।

हाँ: agent से ख़ुद बताने को कहिए। runtime/signals.rs तीन sources को तौलता है। जब osFoundry ख़ुद Claude Code launch करता है, तो runtime/integrations.rs --settings के ज़रिए hooks जोड़ता है। यह flag सिर्फ़ इसी एक launch के लिए settings जोड़ता है, और user के अपने hooks भी चलते रहते हैं।

Claude Code Notification permission prompt के लिए भी fire करता है और input का एक मिनट इंतज़ार करने के बाद भी। इसलिए osf-pane notify payload पढ़ता है और permission को blocked पर और बाक़ी सबको idle पर map करता है। ACP पर (claude.toml में declare किए गए claude-agent-acp adapter के ज़रिए), session/request_permission request का मतलब है कि agent सीधे permission माँग रहा है, यह अनुमान नहीं बल्कि तथ्य है।

दिलचस्प हिस्सा signals::combine का क्रम है। screen से पढ़ा गया blocked हमेशा टिका रहता है। उसके बाद agent की ताज़ा report आती है, फिर "shell वापस सामने है", फिर बाक़ी screen rules। report पुरानी हो सकती है या मौजूद ही न हो, जैसे जब कोई hook चुपचाप fail हो जाए। screen पर दिखता prompt एक सटीक rule है और वही एक alert है जिसे कभी दबाया नहीं जाना चाहिए।

इससे दो छोटे फ़ैसले निकलते हैं। notifications पर हर session और state के लिए 30 s का cooldown है (runtime/notify.rs), क्योंकि redraw होता prompt blocked → working → blocked के बीच झूल सकता है। और कोई भी tool किसी pane में type करे, उससे पहले runtime/tools.rs पिछले sweep पर भरोसा करने के बजाय नया classify_session चलाता है। जो pane blocked है वह सिर्फ़ runtime_answer लेता है, जिसे user confirm करता है, कभी सामान्य runtime_send नहीं।

code चार छोटी फ़ाइलों में है, vt.py, rules.py, fake_agent.py और supervisor.py, साथ में tables के लिए fixtures.py और analyze.py। नतीजा जिस screen पर दिखता है, वह osFoundry डेस्कटॉप ऐप में agent sessions का Sessions board है।

#9821. 5 Common Prescription Drugs Linked To Memory Loss

Prescription drugs taken by millions of people around the world can affect memory.

Prescription drugs taken by millions of people around the world can affect memory.

Memory loss is not always a result of ageing.

Here are five types of drugs that can affect memory.

The older type of antidepressants — known as tricyclics — have been linked to memory loss.

Around half of people taking them report problems concentrating and one-third say they have memory loss.

Benzodiazepines include drugs marketed under the names Valium, Ativan, Klonopin and Xanax.

These drugs are often prescribed for anxiety and other mental health issues such as OCD, insomnia and post-traumatic stress disorder.

Unfortunately they are also linked to memory loss and even Alzheimer’s.

Dr Helene Alphonso, a psychiatrist and Director of Osteopathic Medical Education at Texas University, said:

“Current research is extremely clear and physicians need to partner with their patients to move them into therapies, like [modern] anti-depressants, that are proven to be safer and more effective.”

Statins are prescribed to many people to keep their cholesterol in a safer range.

The Food and Drug Administration lists memory loss, forgetfulness and confusion as possible side-effects of the drug.

Some people do report memory problems when taking them, but the studies conducted so far are inconclusive.

Beta-blockers slow the heart rate and are used to lower blood pressure.

They are also prescribed to those with congestive heart problems.

Beta-blockers, though, may also cause the loss of emotional memories.

They have even been tested as a way of treating post-traumatic stress disorder because of their ability to block emotional memories.

Again, though, the studies are not conclusive.

People who cannot sleep are sometimes prescribed so-called ‘Z-drugs’.

The ‘Z-drugs’ have been linked to memory loss: especially losing the ability to make new memories.

They have also been reported to cause strange behaviours like driving or cooking with absolutely no memory of the event.

Where possible consider a psychological therapy or applicable alternative to using these drugs.

Naturally, you should always consult your physician before making changes to your medication.

Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean

#9818. I can't believe this is how we do stuff now.

I know why I quit coding after a decade of learning, spending countless nights with lots of coffee, and trying to figure things out. I guess I saw it coming, like many others did. We're being replaced more and more by AI, and the way we work is shifting. But what if you don't like being shifted? Haha. I don't.

Anyways, three years later, I came back to give coding another try.

I started experimenting with ChatGPT. Connected it to my newly created repository, offshorts, read some documentation on MDN about how browser extensions work, set up a basic folder structure and asked it to plan things out.

The idea was simple: a browser extension with a toggle button to hide or show YouTube Shorts.

Less than ten minutes later, everything was done. Even published.

Sure, it's a small project, and that was intentional. But it made me stop and think.

I still like knowing how things work. I like looking at the code, understanding the structure and seeing how everything fits together. But I wonder: should I just give in to the "vibe" and forget that the code even exists?

Isn't that vulnerable? What happens if I don't? Will it even matter?

I honestly think nothing makes much sense anymore. And if that's the case, maybe I can just do whatever the fuck I want. Or don't want to do. Including how I work, what I create, and how much of it I actually want to understand.

So here I am. It's a little sad, but I'm back.

#9813. When AI Weight Surgery Met My Daughter's Lazy Eye: A Builder's Notes on Dichoptic VR

The Hacker News thread exploded Tuesday. Astra — weight‑space programming framework, reads and writes neural network weights to steer Qwen without retraining. 2,845 points. 860 comments. I scrolled the discussion at 11 PM, the blue light reflecting off my glasses, thinking about loss functions and gradient descent.

Then my phone buzzed. A photo from my wife: our seven‑year‑old, Mei, wearing an eye patch at the kitchen table. Half‑finished math worksheet. Lower lip trembling.

She’s been patching for fourteen months. Three hours a day. The pediatric ophthalmologist calls it “standard care.”

I stared at the screen, the HN thread still open, the conversation circling around weight‑space surgery — editing a model’s parameters at inference time instead of retraining. The same idea that lets a researcher nudge a language model’s tone could, in theory, nudge a visual cortex’s balance. The dichoptic VR headset we’d been prototyping in the lab already rendered two slightly different scenes, one per eye, at 90 fps. The missing piece was a way to modulate the underlying feature extractor on the fly, per frame, without a full backward pass.

Astra gave exactly that. Its Python API exposes a WeightHandle object that streams the model’s tensors over a lightweight gRPC channel. You ask for a layer, you get a NumPy‑compatible view, you write back, and the next forward pass sees the new values. No checkpoint, no optimizer step, no GPU memory spike. The docs show a one‑liner:

In our case the “model” isn’t a language model but a vision encoder that feeds the dichoptic renderer. The encoder lives on the headset’s edge GPU (a Snapdragon XR2 Gen 2). Astra’s runtime compiles a tiny WebAssembly shim that runs on the same chip, so the weight round‑trip stays under 2 ms — well inside the 11 ms frame budget.

I spent the next two weekends in the garage, the smell of solder and ozone mixing with the faint hum of the headset’s fan. First I dumped the encoder’s projection matrices for the left‑eye and right‑eye streams. They were identical, which explained why Mei’s brain kept suppressing the weaker eye: the network had no incentive to differentiate.

Using Astra’s WeightHandle, I wrote a small controller that adds a contrast bias to the right‑eye pathway — just a 0.3 % scaling on the final 1×1 convolution that maps the encoder’s feature map to the renderer’s texture. The bias is recomputed each frame from a simple heuristic: the current inter‑ocular acuity gap measured by a built‑in eye‑tracker. The code fits in a single file, ~120 lines, and runs entirely on the headset.

The first night we tried it, Mei sat on the couch, headset perched crookedly, the living‑room lamp casting a warm pool on the carpet. She frowned at the floating asteroids — left eye bright, right eye dim — then, after a few seconds, the dim side sharpened. She blinked, turned to me, and whispered, “It’s not blurry anymore.”

That moment wasn’t a clinical trial. It was a single data point, a father watching his daughter’s visual cortex negotiate a new loss landscape in real time. The patch she’d worn for fourteen months stayed on the table, unused for the rest of the evening.

The engineering trade‑offs are worth noting. Astra’s zero‑copy tensor view means we avoid the usual torch.save/torch.load round‑trip that would add ~30 ms latency. The downside: any malformed delta can corrupt the model for the remainder of the session, so we guard every write with a checksum and a rollback path. The headset’s thermal envelope also limits how long we can sustain the extra compute; after ~45 minutes the GPU throttles, and the bias update falls back to a static schedule.

We logged the inter‑ocular contrast threshold before and after each session using the headset’s built‑in psychophysical staircase. Across five evenings the threshold dropped from 0.42 to 0.31 log‑units — a modest shift, but consistent. The numbers are noisy; the sample size is one. Still, the direction matches the hypothesis that targeted weight‑space modulation can rebalance the dichoptic signal without retraining the whole encoder.

What surprised me most was how little code it took to close the loop between a research framework (Astra) and a therapeutic device (the dichoptic VR headset). The same weight‑space primitives that let a hobbyist steer a chatbot’s personality let a clinician steer a visual pathway’s gain. The abstraction held.

Mei still does her patching on weeks when the headset needs charging or when the clinic schedule demands it. But she now asks, “Can we play the asteroid game tonight?” — and the answer is yes, because the game is the therapy.

If you’re building at the intersection of model surgery and real‑time sensory augmentation, the Astra repository is open for experimentation. Join the Discord, share your weight‑space hacks, and let’s see where the next frame takes us.

#9809. Compress to exactly 200 KB: how exact-target image compression works in your browser

Most image compressors give you a quality slider and wish you luck. You pick 80%, export, check the size, and repeat until the file fits under the limit. ToolsByUs Compress Image does it the other way round: you state the target size, and the tool finds the settings that land on it.

The whole thing runs in the browser. The file's contents never leave the tab — there is no upload step at all.

I took a 4032x3024 JPEG photo and asked the tool for exactly 200 KB:

The preview the tool shows is the real encoded result, not a simulation — what you see is the file you download.

A quality slider controls one variable; file size is the outcome of quality, dimensions, format, and image content together. Hitting an exact size means searching that space: try settings, encode, measure, adjust, encode again. Doing that search locally, in the browser, is the interesting engineering part — every encode is real work on your machine, and the tool has to converge without making you wait through dozens of visible attempts.

That is also why the preview matters. If the tool only estimated the size, you would still be guessing. Showing the actual encoded output means the number on screen and the file you download agree.

If you have ever re-exported the same image four times to get under an upload limit, stating the target size up front is the saner workflow. One tool that does it, free, with no upload: https://toolsbyus.com

#9803. Comment osFoundry garde une session Claude Code chaude compatible avec le cache pendant que les messages du canal continuent d'arriver

Voici la deuxième mention que reçoit une session Claude Code résidente dans un canal Message d'osFoundry. C'est le tour utilisateur complet, sans les paragraphes du milieu du brief :

Les champs du payload sont ceux que l'application desktop lit dans agent_session_runtime.rs, avec des valeurs de démo. Le bloc de contexte a été généré par mon portage Python de channel_delivery::render. Ce qu'il laisse de côté compte plus que ce qu'il contient. Pas de system prompt, parce que le processus l'a déjà. Pas de rejeu des tours précédents, parce que le processus s'en souvient. Et aucune ligne du canal que la session a déjà reçue. Ce sont ces trois omissions qui gardent une session de longue durée peu coûteuse. Voici comment chacune fonctionne dans l'application desktop, avec une simulation qui mesure ce qu'elles rapportent.

La résidence se trouve dans runtime/resident.rs. Un processus ACP est maintenu en vie par clé (channel, binding), 4 au maximum en même temps, et tué après 30 minutes d'inactivité. Chaque tour prend un Lease, et Lease::cold est la seule information qui décide de ce qui est envoyé. La branche dans providers/agent_cli.rs se résume à ceci :

prompt vient de build_prompt, qui aplatit toute la conversation en lignes User:/Assistant:. prompt_warm vient de latest_user_turn : le dernier message qui ne vient ni de l'assistant, ni du système, ni d'un outil. Le commentaire dans resident.rs explique pourquoi cet ordre ne se règle pas. Rejouer l'historique dans un processus chaud donnerait à l'agent ses propres réponses passées comme une nouvelle entrée utilisateur à chaque tour, et ça croît de façon quadratique.

Côté prompt caching, c'est la règle du préfixe stable qui fait son travail. Le cadrage système arrive une seule fois, en tête, et ne change jamais. Tout ce qui change d'un tour à l'autre arrive sous forme d'un nouveau tour utilisateur ajouté à la fin.

Dans ce dernier tour utilisateur, après le brief. mention_context récupère les 30 dernières lignes (channel_rows(..., 30)) et les passe à channel_delivery::render avec une limite de 12. La fonction parcourt les lignes dans l'ordre :

Un premier contact reçoit l'en-tête "Recent messages in this channel …". Une session avec watermark reçoit "New messages in this channel since you last heard from it …". S'il n'y a rien de nouveau, aucun bloc n'est envoyé.

Seulement après la réussite du run. render renvoie ce qu'il a affiché, stage() le met de côté sous le canal du run, et le chemin de sortie du run appelle commit() en cas de succès ou discard() en cas d'échec. Le commentaire en donne la raison : un run qui échoue n'a peut-être rien montré à l'agent, et un watermark placé au-delà de ce qu'il a vu masquerait ces messages pour de bon.

Un watermark appartient aussi à une seule session native. L'enregistrement stocké est {native, last_at, ids}, indexé par clé de session, canal et fil, avec 200 ids au maximum, et persisté dans channel-watermarks.json. watermark_for ne le renvoie que si native correspond à l'id du processus qui va répondre maintenant. Après une éviction, un crash ou un Start fresh, le nouveau processus a un nouvel id. Il reçoit donc un nouveau snapshot de 12 messages au lieu d'un trou. Seuls les bindings qui conservent une session ont un watermark : supervisé plus résident, ou une session sauvegardée exacte. Un binding qui repart de zéro à chaque fois reçoit le snapshot à chaque fois, et c'est la seule chose correcte à donner à un processus sans mémoire.

Aucun binaire claude n'est installé sur ce Mac, donc rien ici n'appelle de modèle. sim.py, environ 190 lignes, construit la requête que verrait le fournisseur d'une session chaude à chaque mention :

Le canal contient 200 messages de cinq personnes et d'un agent. 30 d'entre eux mentionnent @claude. Huit sont des logs collés de plus de 600 caractères. Les mentions arrivent par rafales : entre deux, il y a de 1 à 21 messages, avec une médiane de 4. Le brief est le vrai texte de channel_task_brief avec sa partie CLI, soit 466 tokens. PREFIX représente le system prompt d'un CLI plus 20 définitions d'outils, soit 2,120 tokens. C'est plus petit qu'un vrai, mais ce qui compte, c'est qu'il est identique octet pour octet à chaque tour.

Trois stratégies, toutes avec le render / advance porté :

Les tokens sont comptés avec tiktoken cl100k_base, via uv run --with tiktoken. C'est le tokenizer d'OpenAI, pas celui de Claude, donc les valeurs absolues sont approximatives et ce sont les ratios qui comptent. "En cache" désigne le plus long préfixe de tokens commun avec la requête précédente de la même session. Cela suppose que le fournisseur met en cache toute la requête précédente, ce qui est le meilleur cas pour n'importe quelle stratégie. Claude Code place ses propres points de rupture de cache, et ce modèle ne les reproduit pas. "Dupliqués" compte les tokens des lignes du canal que la session avait déjà vues lors d'un tour précédent.

L'exécution complète prend 1.23 s en temps réel sur un Apple M1, surtout pour la tokenisation.

Le watermark ne change pas le ratio de cache. window et watermark restent tous les deux à 0.94. Les lignes du canal répétées se trouvent dans le suffixe de chaque tour, et ce suffixe n'allait de toute façon jamais être en cache. La duplication coûte autre chose. Chaque tour chaud envoie 943 nouveaux tokens au lieu de 766, soit 23% de plus. Et chaque répétition reste ensuite pour toujours dans l'historique de la session, donc la conversation que transporte le CLI grossit plus vite. Sur 30 mentions, la stratégie window a fait passer 516k tokens d'entrée par le fournisseur, contre 417k pour le watermark. L'écart se creuse à chaque tour, parce que chaque requête suivante relit les doublons depuis le cache. Et ça rapproche aussi la compaction.

C'est le préfixe qui décide du cache. Une seule ligne d'état devant le system prompt, 28 tokens qui changent à chaque tour, fait passer la part cacheable de 0.94 à 0.00. Chaque tour chaud devient 14k tokens non cachés au lieu de 766. C'est pour ça qu'osFoundry garde la liste des participants, l'état et les lignes du canal hors du cadrage. La liste des participants et l'activité du projet sont des outils (channel_roster, project_activity), et le texte du canal se trouve dans le tour utilisateur.

Tour par tour, la différence ressemble à ça. À partir de la deuxième mention, window envoie environ 460 tokens de texte du canal, dont 420 à 440 que la session a déjà lus. Le watermark envoie de 21 à 44 tokens.

La façon dont les canaux Message et les agents s'articulent dans l'application est décrite sur la page de détail du canal. Pour comprendre pourquoi un contexte borné compte, voir l'entrée du glossaire sur la fenêtre de contexte.

#9800. Stop Asking LLMs to Do Math: Client-Side Functions in Flutter GenUI with bloc_signals

"An LLM is a phenomenal semantic reasoning engine, but it is an awful, slow, and expensive pocket calculator."

If you haven't watched Andrew "Red" Brogdon's walkthrough on the Flutter channel (Client side functions for Flutter GenUI), stop and watch it. In five minutes, Red exposes the fundamental flaw lurking beneath most early Generative UI demos: the round-trip calculation trap.

Suppose an AI agent generates a recipe or shopping cart card for a user. The user drags a slider to scale the recipe from 2 servings to 6 servings, or edits the quantity of an ingredient.

What happens next in naive GenUI systems?

Making a remote AI call to multiply two numbers on a mobile device equipped with an Apple Silicon or Snapdragon processor capable of billions of operations per second is an architectural anti-pattern.

As Red demonstrated with the Commis kitchen assistant app, the solution is Client-Side Functions: the agent designs the interface and binds expressions, but delegates deterministic execution to local Dart code registered in the client's catalog.

In bloc_signals_genui and bloc_signals_genui_flutter, we have taken this concept to its logical architectural conclusion by pairing Google's official A2UI protocol with synchronous reactive signals.

Running a Dart function locally fixes the latency and token cost of LLM round-trips. But it creates a secondary architectural challenge: how does the UI react when local state changes?

In asynchronous architectures, developers often end up wiring StreamController pipelines, debouncers, or manual setState() callbacks to propagate local math back into generated widgets. Every slider notch pays an event-loop and microtask tax.

Because bloc_signals_genui is built directly on Google's official a2ui_core engine—which natively uses preact_signals—client-side functions are not just callable routines: they are first-class reactive computed() signals.

When a user adjusts a quantity, the calculation runs in the exact same frame. There are zero network round-trips, zero microtask hops, and zero UI flickers.

Here is how you implement and wire client-side functions using bloc_signals_genui.

Subclass FunctionImplementation from bloc_signals_genui (re-exported from a2ui_core). Declare the function's name, return type, and typed JSON argument schema using CommonSchemas.dynamicNumber:

Notice that execute() receives a DataContext. That means your function can read or scope additional local surface state if needed, completely decoupled from Flutter widgets.

Add your function to StandardCatalog using .copyWith(...) and pass it to your A2uiSurfaceBloc:

When your app advertises its capabilities or system prompt to the agent, the agent is informed of calculateCost and its required parameters.

When the AI agent streams down an A2UI JSON component, it doesn't hardcode a static string. Instead, it binds the text property of a Text component to the function call, referencing paths in the local DataModel:

When bloc_signals_genui and bloc_signals_genui_flutter resolve this component, DataContext.resolveSignal() from a2ui_core evaluates the dynamic function call:

In addition to dynamic display properties, client-side functions integrate seamlessly with user actions and remote agent coordination. It is crucial to understand the two distinct operational paths:

When a user taps an interactive component (such as a Button), the client dispatches a SubmitAction event to A2uiSurfaceBloc. The action can either trigger a local client-side function (for example applying a local coupon code or validating form inputs) or emit an A2uiRendererAction outbound to the remote agent:

Generative UI is not a one-way street. A2uiSurfaceBloc provides full bidirectional RPC across the client-agent boundary:

Client-side functions draw a clean, resilient line across your Generative UI architecture:

By adopting Andrew Brogdon's client-side functions pattern and grounding it in a synchronous signal engine, you get the best of both worlds: the creative flexibility of Generative UI with the speed, accuracy, and reliability of native Flutter.

Explore bloc_signals_genui and bloc_signals_genui_flutter on pub.dev, and check out the interactive samples at blocsignal.dev.

#9797. Startup Founder Interview: Brief Is Building the AI CRM Influencer Marketing Teams Have Been Missing

Welcome to HackerNoon’s Writing Prompts! Would you like to take a stab at answering some of these questions? The link for the template is HERE.

Influencer marketing is now a core budget line for most brands, not an experiment. The industry is hitting $47B and the teams running these campaigns are still operating on WhatsApp and spreadsheets. AI finally makes it possible to automate the coordination layer that's been killing their time. Two years ago the AI wasn't good enough. Two years from now every big player will have copied it. Now is the window.

It's just me right now, and that's actually the point. I'm not a developer who discovered influencer marketing. I'm an influencer marketer who learned to build. I've lived inside this problem for 6 years across 1,000+ campaigns and over $5M in spend. I know exactly what breaks, when it breaks, and why. Nobody is closer to this customer than I am because I am the customer.

Honestly? Still managing influencer campaigns and complaining about the lack of good tools. Brief exists because I got tired of waiting for someone else to build it.

Right now, paying customers and retention. I care about teams that come back every month because Brief is how they run their business.

Brief is the AI PM and CRM for influencer marketing teams. It manages campaigns from brief to invoice automatically, it simplifies creator partnerships and content approvals.

I went from building the MVP in under a day, to spending over 100 hours using Lovable, I’m actually on their global 10% users. The speed of that, from idea to live product to first paying customer tells me the demand is real. The exciting part isn't the revenue yet. It's that every team I've shown it to has said the same thing: "I've been looking for this."

50 paying teams by end of year. Then opening the creator workspace, which is a completely different and much larger market. Every creator is running a business: brand deals, content, invoicing, contracts, analytics. Nobody has built the tool that treats it that way.

First customer is a small influencer marketing team, exactly the profile Brief is built for. Over the next 12 months the goal is 50 teams at an average of $799/month.

I don’t se competitors as threats, I study them, and learn from them. The answer to that threat is the same as it's always been: move faster, stay closer to the customer, and build the thing they actually need instead of the thing that looks good in a deck.

As an update: Brief was just accepted at LvlUp Labs Marketing Edge Accelerator, and secured initial funding.

#9792. Top 10 AI Tools in 2023 That Will Make Your Life Easier



 In this article, we explore the top 10 AI tools that are driving innovation and efficiency in various industries. These tools are designed to automate repetitive tasks, improve workflow, and increase productivity. The tools included in our list are some of the most advanced and widely used in the market, and are suitable for a variety of applications. Some of the tools focus on natural language processing, such as ChatGPT and Grammarly, while others focus on image and video generation, such as DALL-E and Lumen5. Other tools such as OpenAI Codex, Tabnine, Canva, Jasper AI,, and Surfer SEO are designed to help with specific tasks such as code understanding content writing and website optimization. This list is a great starting point for anyone looking to explore the possibilities of AI and how it can be applied to their business or project.

So let’s dive into

1. ChatGPT

ChatGPT is a large language model that generates human-like responses to a variety of prompts. It can be used for tasks such as language translation, question answering, and text completion. It can handle a wide range of topics and styles of writing, and generates coherent and fluent text, but should be used with care as it may generate text that is biased, offensive, or factually incorrect.

Pros:

  • Generates human-like responses to a variety of prompts
  • Can be fine-tuned for specific tasks such as language translation, question answering, and text completion
  • Can handle a wide range of topics and styles of writing
  • Can generate coherent and fluent text, even when completing a given text prompt.

Cons:

  • May generate text that is biased or offensive
  • Can generate text that is not accurate or factually correct
  • May require large amounts of computational resources to run
  • The model can sometimes generate text that is not coherent or fluent, depending on the prompt given.

Overall, ChatGPT is a powerful tool for natural language processing, but it should be used with care and with an understanding of its limitations.

2. DALL-E

DALL-E is a generative model developed by OpenAI that is capable of generating images from text prompts. It is based on the GPT-3 architecture, which is a transformer-based neural network language model that has been trained on a massive dataset of text. DALL-E can generate images that are similar to a training dataset and it can generate high-resolution images that are suitable for commercial use.

Pros:

  • Generates high-resolution images
  • Can generate images from text prompts
  • It can be fine-tuned for specific tasks such as generating images of a certain style or category

Cons:

  • May generate images that are not entirely original and could be influenced by the training data
  • May require significant computational resources to run
  • The quality of the generated images may vary depending on the specific prompt

Overall, DALL-E is a powerful AI-based tool for generating images, it can be used for a variety of applications such as creating images for commercial use, gaming, and other creative projects. It is important to note that the generated images should be reviewed and used with care, as they may not be entirely original and could be influenced by the training data.

3. Lumen5

Lumen5 is a content creation platform that uses AI to help users create videos, social media posts, and other types of content. It has several features that make it useful for content creation and marketing, including:

Pros:

  • Automatically summarizes text from a blog post, article, or another source into a script for a video or social media post
  • Offers a library of royalty-free videos, images, and music to use in content
  • Has a drag-and-drop interface for easy content creation
  • Can create videos in multiple languages
  • Has a built-in analytics tool to track the performance of created content.

Cons:

  • The quality of the generated content may vary depending on the source material
  • The automatic summarization feature may not always capture the main points of the source material
  • The library of videos, images, and music is limited.
  • The analytics feature is basic

Overall, Lumen5 is a useful tool for creating content quickly and easily, it can help automate the process of creating videos, social media posts, and other types of content. However, the quality of the generated content may vary depending on the source material and it is important to review and edit the content before publishing it.

4. Grammarly

Grammarly is a writing-enhancement platform that uses AI to check for grammar, punctuation, and spelling errors in the text. It also provides suggestions for improving the clarity, concision, and readability of the text. It has several features that make it useful for improving writing, including:

Pros:

  • Checks for grammar, punctuation, and spelling errors in the text
  • Provides suggestions for improving clarity, concision, and readability
  • Can be integrated with various apps and platforms such as Microsoft Office, Google Docs, and social media platforms
  • Offers a browser extension and a desktop app
  • Has a premium version with more advanced features such as plagiarism detection and more

Cons:

  • The suggestions provided may not always be accurate or appropriate
  • The grammar checker may not always recognize context-specific language use
  • The free version has limited features
  • Limited to English language only
  • Overall, Grammarly is a useful tool for improving writing, it can help users identify and correct grammar and punctuation errors, and improve the clarity, concision, and readability of their text. However, it is important to review the suggestions provided by the tool and use them with caution, as they may not always be accurate or appropriate.

5.OpenAI Codex

OpenAI Codex is a system developed by OpenAI that can create code from natural language descriptions of software tasks. The system is based on the GPT-3 model and can generate code in multiple programming languages.

Pros:

  • Can automate the process of writing code
  • Can help developers to be more productive
  • Can help non-technical people to create software
  • Can generate code in multiple programming languages

Cons:

  • The quality of the generated code may vary depending on the task description
  • The generated code may not always be optimal or efficient
  • The system may not be able to handle complex software tasks
  • Dependence on the tool may lead to a lack of understanding of the code.

Overall, OpenAI Codex is a powerful tool that can help automate the process of writing code and make it more accessible to non-technical people. However, the quality of the generated code may vary depending on the task description and it is important to review and test the code before using it in a production environment. It is important to use the tool as an aid, not a replacement for the developer's knowledge.

6. Tabnine

Tabnine is a code completion tool that uses AI to predict and suggest code snippets. It is compatible with multiple programming languages and can be integrated with various code editors.

Pros:

  • Can improve coding efficiency by suggesting code snippets based on context
  • Can complete entire code blocks
  • Can predict variables, functions, and other elements of code
  • Can be integrated with various code editors

Cons:

  • The suggestions may not always be accurate or appropriate
  • The system may not always be able to understand the context of the code
  • May not work with all code editors
  • Dependence on the tool may lead to a lack of understanding of the code.

Overall, TabNine is a useful tool for developers that can help improve coding efficiency and reduce the time spent on writing code. However, it is important to review the suggestions provided by the tool and use them with caution, as they may not always be accurate or appropriate. It is important to use the tool as an aid, not a replacement for the developer's knowledge.

7. Jasper AI

Jasper is a content writing and content generation tool that uses artificial intelligence to identify the best words and sentences for your writing style and medium in the most efficient, quick, and accessible way.

Pros:

  • User-friendly interface
  • Generates a wide variety of content types
  • Guarantees 100% unique and free-plagiarism content
  • SEO friendly
  •  Create articles of up to 10k words

Cons:

  • Not the cheapest AI writer on the market

8. Surfer SEO

Surfer SEO is a software tool designed to help website owners and digital marketers improve their search engine optimization (SEO) efforts. The tool provides a variety of features that can be used to analyze a website's on-page SEO, including:

Features:

  • A site audit tool that checks for technical SEO issues
  • A content editor that suggests optimizations for individual pages
  • A keyword research tool that suggests keywords to target
  • A SERP analyzer that shows how a website's pages rank for specific keywords
  • A backlink analysis tool that shows the backlinks pointing to a website.

Pros:

  • Can help website owners and marketers identify technical SEO issues
  • Can provide suggestions for optimizing individual pages
  • Can help with keyword research
  • Can show how a website's pages rank for specific keywords
  • Can provide insight into a website's backlink profile

Cons:

  • Some features may require a paid subscription
  • The tool is not a guarantee of better ranking
  • The tool can only analyze the data it has access to
  • The tool's suggestions may not always be applicable or optimal

Overall, Surfer SEO can be a useful tool for website owners and digital marketers looking to improve their SEO efforts. However, it is important to remember that it is just a tool and should be used in conjunction with other SEO best practices. Additionally, the tool is not a guarantee of better ranking.

9. Zapier

Zapier is a web automation tool that allows users to automate repetitive tasks by connecting different web applications together. It does this by creating "Zaps" that automatically move data between apps, and can also be used to trigger certain actions in one app based on events in another app.

Features:

  • Can connect over 3,000 web applications
  • Can automate repetitive tasks
  • Can create "Zaps" to move data between apps
  • Can trigger certain actions in one app based on events in another app.

Pros:

  • Can automate repetitive tasks
  • Can save time
  • Can improve workflow
  • Can increase productivity
  • Can be integrated with a wide range of web applications

Cons:

  • Can be difficult to set up
  • May require some technical skills
  • May require a paid subscription for some features
  • Some apps may not be compatible
  • Dependence on the tool may lead to a lack of understanding of the apps

Overall, Zapier is a useful tool that can help users automate repetitive tasks and improve workflow. It can save time and increase productivity by connecting different web applications together. However, it may require some technical skills and some features may require a paid subscription. It is important to use the tool with caution and not to rely too much on it, to understand the apps better.

10. Compose AI

Compose AI is a company that specializes in developing natural language generation (NLG) software. Their software uses AI to automatically generate written or spoken text from structured data, such as spreadsheets, databases, or APIs.

Features:

  • Automatically generates written or spoken text from structured data
  • Can be integrated with a wide range of data sources
  • Can be used for a variety of applications such as creating reports, summaries, and explanations
  • Provides an API and a user-friendly interface

Pros:

  • Can help users create more accurate and consistent content
  • Can help users save time by automating repetitive tasks
  • Can be integrated with a wide range of data sources

Cons:

  • The generated content may not always be optimal or efficient

Overall, Compose AI's NLG software can be a useful tool for automating the process of creating written or spoken content from structured data. However, the quality of the generated content may vary depending on the data source, and it is essential to review the generated content before using it in a production environment. It is important to use the tool as an aid, not a replacement for the understanding of the data.

Conclusion

The top 10 AI tools included in this article are some of the most advanced and widely used in the market, and are suitable for various applications. #9779. The best apples for apple pie: Here's how to choose.: We put six varieties to the test.

Which are the best pie apples? With apple-picking season hard upon us, it's time to dust off your favorite apple pie recipe, sharpen your crust-rolling skills, and get ready to enjoy fall's favorite dessert: apple pie.

You may be tempted to make your pie from one of the six apple varieties that dominate the domestic market year-round: Red Delicious, Golden Delicious, Gala, Fuji, Granny Smith, and McIntosh.

But when fall rolls around, farmers' markets and orchard farm stands offer an abundance of apple choices.

You've probably identified your favorite eating apple. But what about the best pie apples? They're not necessarily the same. Red and Golden Delicious, for instance, are reliably crisp, sweet-eating apples. But when you bake them into a pie, they can become mushy and lose some of their sweetness. So what are the best apples for pie?

We'll put six different pie apples to the test.

The pie apples: I decide to put two of my favorites, Golden Russet and Northern Spy, up against a couple of classic pie apples: McIntosh and Cortland. I also add Granny Smith because, if there's one ubiquitous, year-round apple, Granny Smith is it. Ginger Gold — a Golden Delicious cross with Albemarle Pippin — is another variety that's often available in fall, and a worthy representative of the Delicious family.

And yes, there are plenty of other apple varieties to choose from: Fuji, Gala, Honey Crisp, and so many more. But with limited time and resources — and a pan with space for just six pies — I'm not able to test every apple out there. But if you want to choose the best pie apples among your personal favorites, you can have fun doing this same test at home.

I use a muffin tin to bake apples sweetened with a bit of sugar. To mimic apple pie (sans crust), I pile sliced apples high in the pan. Then I bake them in a preheated 425°F oven for 20 minutes, lower the oven temperature to 375°F, and continue to bake the apples until they're bubbly, about 40 minutes.

I had no idea there'd be such significant differences in both texture and flavor. For example, Russets and Macs are sweetened with the same amount of sugar, bake at the same temperature, for the same amount of time —  and offer way different results.

So, Granny Smith looks like the best combination of both taste and texture. Does it make the very best apple pie?

Not necessarily. I've baked many pies with this all-purpose apple, especially during the winter when other apples are scarce or pricey. A pie made 100% with Granny Smith apples is a mighty fine pie. But in fall, when every apple variety in the world is seemingly at your fingertips, why not take advantage of one or two (or more) of your own local favorites?

At the end of the day, choosing the best pie apples is a personal decision. My best apple pie would include a combination of these three: Cortland, for flavor; Russet, for texture; and Granny Smith, for its combination of the two.

What apples would fill your best pie? Bake your favorite varieties side by side and see what happens; the results may surprise you.

Please share your favorite apples for pie — and your favorite apple pie tips! — in comments, below.

#9775. How to prebake pie crust — and why you should: The key to flaky — not flabby — pie crust.

A soggy bottom. Not something you want for your baby. Or your pie crust. And while we can’t help you with your baby, there’s a simple solution to pies with soggy bottoms: prebake (also known as blind bake) the crust.

There are a number of reasons your pie can end up with a soft, pale, underbaked crust — and steps you can take to help prevent that unfortunate result.

But the one surefire way to make certain your pie’s crust will be golden brown, crisp, and delicious — just as appealing as its filling — is to prebake it. That’s right: bake the bottom crust first, before adding the filling.

Most commonly, it's smart to prebake pie crust when:

But some fillings might instead cook fully on the stovetop, like the rich, thick filling for chocolate cream pie. When it’s done, you simply pour it into its crust — and said crust had better be prebaked to perfection, since the pie’s not going anywhere near an oven.

Other pies, typically those with a more delicate, egg- and cream-based filling (think custard pie or quiche) require at least some baking — but don’t spend long enough in the oven (at a high enough temperature) to guarantee a fully baked, brown and crispy crust.

In these cases, you need to prebake your crust.

The recipe you're following may explain explicitly how to prebake your crust. But if it doesn't, follow this process:

First, roll your bottom crust and place it in the pan. Crimp or flatten the edge. Chill it for 30 minutes, to relax the gluten and firm up the fat(s); this will help prevent shrinkage, so don't skip!

Line the crust with foil, parchment, or a paper coffee filter. Fill it about two-thirds full with dried beans, uncooked rice (or other uncooked grain berries), pie weights, or granulated sugar.

Bake the crust in a preheated 375°F oven for 20 minutes, set on a baking stone or steel if you have one. Remove the crust from the oven and lift out the liner and weights. (If you’ve used sugar, save it for your future baking; it’ll be lightly toasted and yummy!)

At this point your crust is partially prebaked, and good for any of your pies that tend to exhibit a wan, flabby bottom crust when done. Think pumpkin pie: You don’t want to bake the filling so long that it’s stiff and dry, but you may pull your pie out of the oven to find your perfectly baked filling is resting in a partially baked crust. Prebaking your crust partway is a sensible solution for this scenario.

To fully prebake the crust, prick the bottom all over with a fork to prevent bubbles. Return the crust to the oven and bake for an additional 20 to 25 minutes, until it’s golden all over.

If, despite your best efforts, the lined, weighted crust still slips down the inside of the pan while it prebakes, try this: Bake the crust upside down.

To start, you’ll need two identical (or nicely nestable) pie pans with flat rims.

Place your rolled-out crust in one of the pans, anchoring it to the rim of the pan with a fork-tine crimp. Place a liner of some kind (same as above: parchment, foil, coffee filter) into the pan. Nest the second pan into the first.

Pick up both pans, turn them over, and set them on a baking sheet. Place the baking sheet and pie pans in the oven, and bake as directed above. As the crust bakes, gravity will pull it down toward its rim — rather than into a puddle at the bottom of the pan. Magic!

After 20 minutes remove the baking sheet from the oven, carefully turn the pans over, lift out the empty pan, and remove the liner. At this point, your crust is partially prebaked. To prebake it fully, place the crust back in the oven, right side up, and bake until it's golden.

If you struggle with a pale, pasty bottom crust in your fruit pie, then yes, you can prebake it — with a couple of caveats:

So, soggy bottoms begone! From now on I expect every pie you bake will have a deep golden brown, flaky, crispy crust on the bottom — all because of the prebake.

And if you have any other questions about pie — from creating tender, flaky crust to thickening fruit filling to assessing when your pie is perfectly baked — please check out our Pie Baking Guide.
